title: Midlatitude Cirrus Clouds and Multiple Tropopauses from a 2002-2006  Climatology over the SIRTA Observatory
direct_prompt: Midlatitude cirrus clouds, characterized by thin, wispy structures, play a pivotal role in Earth's climate system by modulating the radiation budget. The co-occurrence of multiple tropopauses, as observed over the Southern Great Plains (SGP) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Program site, has implications for understanding the characteristics of cirrus clouds and their radiative effects. By analyzing a 2002-2006 climatology constructed from the ARM micropulse lidar (MPL), we present a detailed investigation of the seasonal and diurnal variations in midlatitude cirrus clouds and their relationships with the temperature and water vapor structures in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS). The results indicate that midlatitude cirrus clouds exhibit distinct seasonal and diurnal variations in frequency of occurrence, cloud base and top heights, and optical properties. These variations are closely associated with the temperature and water vapor variations in the UTLS, such as the height of cold point tropopause (CPT), lapse rates within 2 km above and below the CPT, and water vapor mixing ratio above the CPT. Our study provides insights into the complex interactions between cirrus clouds and the UTLS thermal and water vapor structures and improves the parameterizations of cirrus clouds in the general circulation models (GCMs).
prompt_few_shot: Midlatitude cirrus clouds play an important role in the Earth's climate system as they influence the Earth's radiative balance and modulate the transport of water vapor from the troposphere to the stratosphere. Based on 5 years of continuous middle-atmospheric temperature measurements obtained by the ground-based microwave radiometer SIRTA (Stratospheric and InfraRed Tropospheric Absorption spectrometer) in the subtropical free troposphere (Reunion Island, 20.9°S, 55.5°E), we present a detailed climatology of cirrus clouds and multiple tropopauses. The cirrus climatology derived from SIRTA is in good agreement with spaceborne lidar observations. In addition, our results highlight the ability of SIRTA to characterize the thermal and dynamical structure of the upper troposphere/lower stratosphere (UTLS) region. We find that most of the cirrus clouds are semi-transparent and exhibit mean ice water contents of about 30 mg m−3. During the summer season, multiple tropopauses are observed about 15% of the time and more than 40% of these multiple tropopauses exhibit a "low-to-high" thermal tropopause structure. The dynamical control of the lower branch of the "low-to-high" tropopauses by Rossby wave breaking is supported by our trajectory calculations.
prompt_SICO: **Abstract:** This study presents a six-year climatology (2002–2006) of midlatitude cirrus clouds and multiple tropopauses over the Southern Italy Tropospheric Observatory (38.2°N, 16.5°E). Cirrus cloud occurrence frequency, cloud top height, and cloud geometrical and optical thickness are derived from ground-based lidar and radar measurements. The results show a large seasonal variability with a maximum of cirrus occurrence frequency in summer and a minimum in winter. In summer, the cirrus cloud geometrical thickness increases from about 1.0 km in the morning to about 2.0 km in the afternoon. This increase is mainly explained by the diurnal cycle of deep convection. Cirrus clouds in summer are mainly composed of small ice crystals with a mean effective radius of about 20 μm. In winter, a secondary maximum of cirrus occurrence frequency is observed in the early morning hours, which is associated with the frequent occurrence of multiple tropopauses. The dynamical tropopause is on average 2–3 km higher than the thermal tropopause, and the layer between the two tropopauses contains cirrus clouds with large ice crystals (mean effective radius of about 50 μm).

title: Emission and absorption noise in the fractional quantum Hall effect
direct_prompt: Here is a 6 sentence abstract for the provided article title:The fractional quantum Hall effect occurs at low temperatures when a two-dimensional electron system is exposed to a strong perpendicular magnetic field. In this regime, the emergence of fractional quantum numbers such as fractional charge and statistics leads to fascinating phenomena. In this work, we investigate emission and absorption noise processes in this exotic topological state of matter. Using theoretical calculations and numerical simulations, we show that noise measurements can reveal clues about the underlying quasi-particle excitations that govern transport properties. The possible fractional charge of such excitations leaves a distinct signature in the energy and temperature dependence of the noise. title: Bibliometric statistical properties of the 100 largest European  universities: prevalent scaling rules in the science system
direct_prompt: This study investigates bibliometric statistical properties of the 100 largest European universities, focusing on prevalent scaling rules in the science system. The analysis was based on data compiled from various academic databases, including publication output, citation counts, and authorship patterns. By examining these properties, we aimed to gain insights into the research performance and impact of these institutions in the scientific community. Our results revealed a significant correlation between the size of the universities and their publication and citation counts, indicating a scaling effect in the science system. Additionally, we found that the distribution of publications and citations followed a power-law distribution, suggesting the presence of universal patterns in the dissemination of scientific knowledge. The authorship patterns of the universities showed a high degree of collaboration both within and outside the institutions, highlighting the importance of interdisciplinary research in academic productivity. Furthermore, our analysis revealed a positive correlation between the universities' research output and their international collaboration, indicating the benefits of global networking in research activities. Interestingly, we observed variations in the scaling rules among different scientific disciplines, suggesting discipline-specific factors influencing research performance. Overall, our study provides valuable insights into the bibliometric properties of European universities and the underlying scaling rules in the science system. These findings can inform policy makers, funding agencies, and academic institutions in promoting research excellence and collaboration within the European scientific community.

direct_prompt: Here is a 7 sentence abstract for the provided article title:Cloud cores play an important role in star formation as they must collapse under their own gravity to form protostars. Previous studies have shown cloud cores can form through dynamic compressions from supersonic turbulent motions in molecular clouds. In this study, we conduct 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations to model the formation and evolution of quiescent cloud cores induced by dynamic compressions. Our results demonstrate that transient compressions are capable of forming quasi-stable, quiescent cloud cores embedded in supersonic turbulent flows. However, we find these dynamically-formed cloud cores are inherently ephemeral, with most collapsing back into the ambient turbulent gas within only a few million years. Nevertheless, a small fraction are able to achieve stable, quasi-hydrostatic equilibrium and may persist long enough for gravitational collapse to initiate star formation. Our work provides new insights into the short-lived nature of dynamically-formed quiescent cloud cores in turbulent molecular clouds.

These applications require Quality-of-Service (QoS) guarantees for satisfactory user experience. This paper proposes an energy-efficient resource allocation scheme for wireless networks to meet QoS constraints of users while minimizing energy consumption. The scheme formulates the resource allocation problem as a non-convex optimization problem with QoS and energy efficiency criteria. An iterative algorithm is developed using convex relaxation and decomposition techniques to find a near-optimal solution. Simulation results show that the proposed scheme reduces energy consumption by up to 30% compared to baseline schemes, while still satisfying average delay and outage probability constraints. By intelligently matching transmit power and subcarrier allocation, the method provides an effective approach to balance energy efficiency and satisfactory QoS support in wireless systems. The resource allocation scheme has the potential to lower network operational costs and carbon footprint without degrading user experience.

Through simulations, we demonstrate that the proposed pseudo-random puncturing technique effectively reduces the error floor of turbo codes, making them more robust in noisy communication environments. Overall, our results show that pseudo-random puncturing is a promising approach to enhance the reliability of turbo codes in practical applications.

By solving the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, we obtain the ground-state phase diagrams of the system for different interaction strengths and rotation speeds. The phase-locked state is characterized by a well-defined number of vortices in each component, which is proportional to the rotation speed. We also calculate the excitation spectrum of the system and find that the phase-locked state is dynamically stable. Our results provide a theoretical understanding of the recent experiments on vortex lattice locking in rotating two-component Bose-Einstein condensates.

title: Scintillator Tile Hadron Calorimeter with Novel SiPM Readout
direct_prompt: Here is an 8 sentence abstract for the given title:Calorimeters are essential detectors at particle colliders to measure jet and missing transverse energy. This paper presents the development of a novel scintillator tile hadron calorimeter with silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readout. The detector consists of polystyrene scintillator tiles interleaved with steel absorber plates in a sampling calorimeter structure. Each tile is read out by wavelength shifting fibers coupled to an array of SiPM devices. The SiPMs offer advantages over traditional photomultiplier tubes, including insensitivity to magnetic fields, compact size, and stability of response. Tests of the tile-fiber-SiPM unit showed peak light detection efficiency above 50%. A full-scale prototype cassette housing 20 tiles was assembled and tested with particle beams, demonstrating energy linearity better than 5% across the energy range. The results validate this SiPM-based calorimeter concept for future collider experiments and indicate its potential for compact integration into the magnetic volumes of particle detectors.
prompt_few_shot: Here is an 8 sentence abstract for the given academic article title:An analog scintillator tile hadron calorimeter (AHCAL) prototype has been constructed with a novel silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readout scheme. The AHCAL consists of 38 layers of steel plates interleaved with plastic scintillator tiles read out by wavelength-shifting fibers coupled to arrays of SiPMs. A custom application-specific integrated circuit chip was designed to amplify and shape the signals from the SiPMs. A calibration system using LED light monitors the SiPM gain and measures the full response curve to correct for non-linearity effects. Tests of the AHCAL in particle beams aim to study hadronic shower shapes and test the concept of particle flow calorimetry. The performance and reliability of over 7,000 SiPM channels will be evaluated. The prototype will be commissioned in beams at CERN and Fermilab to record hadronic, electromagnetic and muon showers over a range of energies and incident angles. This novel SiPM readout scheme holds promise for application in highly granular calorimeters proposed for future collider detectors.
prompt_SICO: Here is an 8 sentence academic abstract in a style similar to human writings:We present the design and performance of a scintillator tile hadron calorimeter instrumented with an innovative silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readout. The calorimeter consists of alternating layers of plastic scintillator tiles and steel absorber plates. Each 2.6 x 2.6 x 15 cm scintillator tile is read out by four SiPM arrays mounted on the Tile Calorimeter module front-end boards. The SiPM arrays were specially developed for this application featuring low crosstalk, small pixel size, and integrated quenching resistors. Test beam measurements with protons show that the calorimeter achieves an energy resolution of 50%/√E⊕ 2.5% and timing resolution better than 2 ns. Detailed comparisons with Geant4 simulations demonstrate excellent matching of longitudinal and lateral shower profiles. This correlation is caused by the fact that star-forming galaxies produce large amounts of ionizing radiation, which heats and ionizes the surrounding IGM. This ionized IGM emits 21cm radiation, which can be detected by radio telescopes. Our results suggest that the 21cm emission can be used to trace the star formation history of the universe.

On large scales, the correlation is weaker, as the 21cm emission is more affected by the large-scale structure of the Universe. Our results suggest that the 21cm emission can be used to trace the history of star formation during the reionization epoch.

title: Prospects of medium tomography using hard processes inside a soft medium
direct_prompt: Here is a 7 sentence academic article abstract for the given title:Medium tomography using alternative hard processes holds promise to reveal new insights into complex soft materials. Previous tomographic techniques relying on scattering or absorption have encountered limitations in resolving intricate structures within soft unconsolidated media. This paper presents a novel approach utilizing induced hard particle reactions within a soft material to act as location markers readable by tomography. Simulations demonstrate high-energy particle beams can initiate localized hardening to produce distinctive spots identifiable in subsequent scans. Preliminary phantom experiments show clear detection of simulated reaction sites down to the sub-millimeter scale. Our results suggest this method may offer improved resolution over traditional techniques. Further refinements and tests are still needed but the prospects of medium tomography using hard processes inside a soft medium appear favorable.

Medium-induced radiative and elastic scattering modifies the development of jets as they traverse the produced medium. This paper explores using such modifications to extract information about the properties of the underlying medium. A Monte Carlo model is developed to simulate the in-medium shower evolution of jets including both pQCD-based collisional energy loss and medium-induced bremsstrahlung. The model uses a realistic hydrodynamic simulation of the spacetime evolution of the quark-gluon plasma as input. Several jet observables are investigated for their sensitivity to properties of the medium like density and transport coefficient. It is found that comparing data for such quantities to model calculations holds promise for three-dimensional tomographic imaging of the quark-gluon plasma.

title: The dust distribution in edge-on galaxies. Radiative transfer fits of V  and K'-band images
direct_prompt: The dust distribution in edge-on galaxies. Radiative transfer fits of V and K'-band imagesWe present a study of the dust distribution in edge-on galaxies using radiative transfer fits of V and K'-band images. The sample consists of 12 nearby galaxies with a wide range of morphological types. We use a two-dimensional dust distribution model to fit the observed images, and we derive the dust opacity, scale height, and asymmetry. The dust distribution is also found to be asymmetric in most of the galaxies, with the dust lane being shifted towards the north-east. We compare our results with those of previous studies, and we discuss the implications of our findings for the dust properties and evolution in edge-on galaxies.

human_text: A quantum system composed of two or more subsystems can be in an entangledstate, i.e. a state in which the properties of the global system are welldefined but the properties of each subsystem are not. Entanglement is at theheart of quantum physics, both for its conceptual foundations and forapplications in information processing and quantum communication. Remarkably,entanglement can be "swapped": if one prepares two independent entangled pairsA1-A2 and B1-B2, a joint measurement on A1 and B1 (called a "Bell-StateMeasurement", BSM) has the effect of projecting A2 and B2 onto an entangledstate, although these two particles have never interacted or shared any commonpast[1,2]. Experiments using twin photons produced by spontaneous parametricdown-conversion (SPDC) have already demonstrated entanglement swapping[3-6],but here we present its first realization using continuous wave (CW) sources,as originally proposed[2]. The challenge was to achieve sufficiently sharpsynchronization of the photons in the BSM. Using narrow-band filters, thecoherence time of the photons that undergo the BSM is significantly increased,exceeding the temporal resolution of the detectors. Hence pulsed sources can bereplaced by CW sources, which do not require any synchronization[6,7], allowingfor the first time the use of completely autonomous sources. Our experimentexploits recent progress in the time precision of photon detectors, in theefficiency of photon pair production by SPDC with waveguides in nonlinearcrystals[8], and in the stability of narrow-band filters. This approach isindependent of the form of entanglement; we employed time-bin entangledphotons[9] at telecom wavelengths. Our setup is robust against thermal ormechanical fluctuations in optical fibres thanks to cm-long coherence lengths.

title: On reverberation and cross-correlation estimates of the size of the  broad-line region in active galactic nuclei
direct_prompt: Here is a 13 sentence abstract for the provided article title:The broad-line region (BLR) in active galactic nuclei (AGN) is a important component that provides clues about the physics around supermassive black holes. This study examines reverberation mapping and cross-correlation techniques to estimate the size of the BLR using optical and ultraviolet emission lines. Reverberation mapping relies on the time delay between variations in the continuum emission and the responding variations seen in emission lines arising from the BLR. Cross-correlation estimates the time delay by quantifying the similarity between light curves as a function of time lag. This work utilizes archival photometric and spectroscopic monitoring data from international ground and space-based observatories of 11 AGNs over several months to years. Detailed cross-correlation analysis is performed between the ultraviolet/optical continuum and prominent broad emission lines of hydrogen, helium, and carbon. The cross-correlation peaks provide Size-Luminosity relationships for the BLR as a function of line species. Robust uncertainty measurements are derived through simulated light curves and flux randomization methods. The sizes found through cross-correlation generally agree with previous reverberation mapping results but with improved precision thanks to the long temporal baselines of the data. Comparisons between lines suggest stratification of the BLR depending on ionization level. Overall, this study demonstrates that cross-correlation techniques can reliably estimate BLR sizes and help refine photoionization models of the region without needing extensive spectroscopic campaigns. The methods explored here can be applied to future large optical imaging and spectroscopic surveys to characterize AGN populations and black hole growth over cosmic time.

We explore an alternative approach that models the light curves directly using stochastic processes to recover time lags and associated uncertainties. We apply this method to archival monitoring data for 87 emission lines in 31 quasars. Preliminary results confirm past size-luminosity relationships, with some notable exceptions that motivate further investigation. Ultimately, this research sheds light on the complex interplay between stellar dynamics and mass distribution within globular clusters.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methodology through a series of computational experiments, showing that it can generate a wide range of complex 3D structures, including hierarchical, branching, and heterogeneous structures. The proposed methodology has potential applications in various fields, such as tissue engineering, regenerative medicine, and bio-inspired design.

In this picture, superconductivity arises from the condensation of these bosons. The doped-carrier theory, on the other hand, treats the CuO2 planes as a conventional metal with a high density of charge carriers. In this picture, superconductivity arises from the pairing of these carriers by the exchange of magnetic fluctuations.Both theories provide a good description of many of the experimental properties of high-Tc superconductors. However, there are some key differences between the two theories. The slave-boson theory predicts that the superconducting transition temperature should be proportional to the square root of the doping level, while the doped-carrier theory predicts that it should be proportional to the doping level itself. The slave-boson theory also predicts that the Hall coefficient should be positive, while the doped-carrier theory predicts that it should be negative.These differences between the two theories have been the subject of much debate in the literature. The slave-boson theory is generally considered to be more successful in describing the properties of high-Tc superconductors, but the doped-carrier theory is simpler and more intuitive. Further experiments are needed to determine which theory is ultimately correct.

title: Clustering Co-occurrence of Maximal Frequent Patterns in Streams
direct_prompt: Here is an 11 sentence abstract for the given article title:Stream clustering has become increasingly important for analyzing real-time data. This article presents a novel approach for clustering the co-occurrence of maximal frequent patterns in data streams. Frequent pattern mining is applied to generate maximal frequent patterns from each sliding window of the stream. The co-occurrence relationship between patterns is then represented as a graph structure. A graph clustering algorithm is adapted to group similar patterns together based on their co-occurrence links. This allows patterns in the stream to be grouped according to their common attributes and behaviors over time. The algorithm is fully incremental and able to dynamically update the clustering as new windows of data arrive. An experimental evaluation demonstrates that the clustering can effectively discover meaningful pattern groups from synthetic and real data streams. The memory and time complexity of the algorithm is also analyzed. Several parameter sensitivity tests are performed to understand their impact on clustering quality. Finally, potential applications of the clustered patterns in ranking, classification and anomaly detection are discussed. The proposed approach offers an effective way to analyze and monitor evolving patterns in high-speed streams.

Then a clustering algorithm is applied to group patterns that frequently co-occur together over time. Experimental evaluations on both synthetic and real-world data streams demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed clustering approach. The identified clusters of related patterns can provide useful insights into the underlying dynamics and changes in streaming data. Additionally, monitoring pattern co-occurrence over time enables detecting emerging trends and capturing concept drift. In summary, this work makes an important first step toward understanding the collective behavior of frequent patterns in data streams.

Our results provide a valuable insight into the growth of heteroepitaxial QDs and pave the way for the realization of ordered QD arrays with desired properties.

In this paper, we undertake a travelling wave analysis to investigate the effects of convection on the emergence of limit cycles. Through numerical simulations, we modeled a reaction-diffusion system undergoing convection and observed recurrent oscillatory patterns. We then performed a linear stability analysis to analyze the conditions under which the system exhibited absolute and convective instabilities. Our results show that convection induces a saddle point structure that can either suppress or amplify oscillatory instabilities depending on parameter values. We identify precise convection thresholds beyond which the system transitions fromabsolute to convective instability. Using front evolution equations, we further characterize the propagation speed and deformation of oscillatory convective fronts. Finally, we discuss implications of our findings for applications involving thermal oscillations, chemical waves, and population dynamics in flowing environments.Our travelling wave analysis provides new insights into how natural and fluid convection influence the emergence and dynamics of limit cycle oscillations.

We report on the results of this search and derive upper limits on the muon neutrino fluence from GRBs. We consider GRB models that predict a large flux of high-energy neutrinos. The resulting upper limits provide significant constraints on these models. The new upper limits are a significant improvement over the previously published limits from the AMANDA experiment.

direct_prompt: **Abstract:**Quantum zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) are a powerful tool for proving the knowledge of a secret without revealing any information about it. They have a number of advantages over classical ZKPs, including their ability to prove statements about quantum states and their resistance to attack by quantum computers. In this paper, we study the general properties of quantum ZKPs. We first introduce the basic concepts of quantum information theory and quantum cryptography. We then define quantum ZKPs and discuss their advantages over classical ZKPs. We also present a number of new results on the properties of quantum ZKPs, including their completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge properties. Finally, we discuss some potential applications of quantum ZKPs.
prompt_few_shot: General Properties of Quantum Zero-Knowledge ProofsAbstract: We give a detailed introduction to the general properties of quantum zero-knowledge proofs, which includes completeness, soundness, and zero-knowledge properties. The completeness requires that if a prover has a witness, he can convince the verifier with an overwhelming probability. The soundness demands that if a prover has no witness, the probability of the verifier accepting is negligible. Zero-knowledge means that the verifier learns nothing about the witness except for the fact that it exists. We prove that quantum zero-knowledge proofs satisfy all these properties under the assumption that the underlying quantum systems are isolated and measurements are non-disturbing. In particular, we show that in the quantum setting, the completeness can be perfect and the zero-knowledge property holds in the information-theoretic sense, even for entangled provers, which are fundamentally different from the classical case. Finally, we discuss some of the potential applications of quantum zero-knowledge proofs.

title: Dbar-N interaction from meson-exchange and quark-gluon dynamics
direct_prompt: Here is a 6 sentence abstract for the given article title:We investigate the interaction between antibaryons (Dbar) and nucleons (N) using different theoretical models. Previous studies have largely relied on meson-exchange models to describe the forces between Dbar and N at hadronic scales. In this work, we develop a quantum chromodynamics motivated model that incorporates quark and gluon degrees of freedom to account for Dbar-N dynamics from a more fundamental perspective. Our model calculates scattering amplitudes by representing the Dbar and N as valance quarks embedded in a sea of quasi-free gluons. Preliminary results indicate that quark-gluon effects produce an attractive Dbar-N potential comparable in strength to meson exchanges at intermediate distances. Precise measurements of Dbar-N scattering could help discriminate between the meson-exchange and quark-gluon descriptions of the interaction and provide new insights into the role of quarks and gluons in baryonic systems.

Coupling to open charm channels such as pi-Λc and pi-Σc is also taken into account. The short distance interaction arising from quark-gluon dynamics is modeled using constraints from QCD such as heavy quark symmetry. The full interaction model is used to dynamically generate the Λc(2595) resonance as a DbarN quasi-bound state. Results for DbarN total and differential cross sections are obtained and compared to predictions from models based only on meson exchange or only on quark-gluon dynamics.

title: Mapping the circumstellar SiO maser emission in R Leo
direct_prompt: SiO maser emission has long been recognized as a valuable tool for studying the circumstellar environments of evolved stars, particularly in the case of Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stars like R Leo. In this study, we present high-resolution maps of the SiO maser emission in the circumstellar envelope of R Leo using the Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) technique. The maps reveal a complex and asymmetric distribution of SiO maser spots, with multiple components distributed over a wide range of radial velocities. We find evidence for a low-velocity component of SiO maser emission that is concentrated in the inner regions of the circumstellar envelope, as well as a high-velocity component that extends to larger distances. The high-resolution maps also reveal a strong correlation between the SiO maser emission and the distribution of dust emission in the circumstellar envelope, indicating a close spatial relationship between the maser-emitting gas and the dusty material. Our results suggest that the SiO maser emission in R Leo is likely produced in regions of enhanced density and temperature, such as shocks or dense clumps in the circumstellar envelope. The asymmetry of the maser distribution may reflect the presence of non-spherical structures or mass-loss mechanisms in R Leo. Overall, our study provides important insights into the physical conditions and dynamics of the circumstellar environment of R Leo, shedding light on the processes driving the mass loss and evolution of AGB stars.

title: Star Formation in the Bok Globule CB54
direct_prompt: This paper presents a study on the star formation activity within the Bok Globule CB54, a dense, compact molecular cloud located in the constellation Cygnus. Through observations using the Spitzer Space Telescope, we identified several young stellar objects embedded within the globule. Analysis of the data revealed the presence of protostars and candidate pre-main sequence stars within CB54, indicating ongoing star formation in this region. We also investigated the physical properties of the globule, such as its mass, temperature, and density, to better understand the conditions conducive to star formation. Our findings suggest that CB54 is a promising site for further studies on the early stages of star formation. The results of this research contribute to our understanding of the complex processes involved in the formation of stars within molecular clouds. Future observations with higher resolution instruments will provide additional insights into the mechanisms driving star formation in this intriguing region.

title: Validating module network learning algorithms using simulated data
direct_prompt: Here is a 9 sentence academic abstract for the provided title:Module network learning algorithms attempt to identify modules, or groups of densely interconnected nodes, within complex network data. However, evaluating the quality and accuracy of these algorithms is challenging without ground truth about the underlying modular structure. In this paper, we develop a framework for systematically validating module detection algorithms using simulated benchmark networks. We generate random networks with planted modular structures of varying complexity and evaluate several state-of-the-art module learning methods on their ability to recover these artificially encoded communities. Our results show that recent methods based on optimizing statistical metrics are generally effective at identifying planted modules when modules are of sufficient size and density. However, their performance decreases for small, weakly defined modules that more closely mimic the structures found in real-world data. We also analyze how algorithm performance varies with network size, noise level, and other empirical network properties. Overall, our study provides a quantitative baseline for comparing module learning algorithms and informs how they should be applied and interpreted on empirical network data.

However, these methods are difficult to thoroughly evaluate due to the lack of fully known real-world networks. In this work, we generate in silico simulated expression data from well-defined transcriptional regulatory networks. This allows us to systematically test different module learning algorithms in a controlled setting where the ground truth is known. Using benchmark expression profiles paired with known network structure, we compare a module-based algorithm against a direct inference approach. Analysis of precision and recall reveals the relative strengths and limitations of each method for recovering different aspects of the true underlying network. The modular structure is better identified while direct approaches recover more local regulator-target relations. Validation on this simulated data provides critical insights for evaluating network inference techniques.

title: Constraints on the Abundance of Highly Ionized Proto-Cluster Regions  from the Absence of Large Voids in the Lyman Alpha Forest
direct_prompt: Constraints on the Abundance of Highly Ionized Proto-Cluster Regions from the Absence of Large Voids in the Lyman Alpha ForestABSTRACT: We investigate the constraints imposed by the absence of large voids in the observed Lyman alpha forest (Lyman alpha forest) on the abundance of highly ionized proto-cluster regions. We use a simple model to estimate the expected number of voids as a function of the filling factor and clumping properties of the ionized regions. We find that the observed abundance of voids places strong constraints on the volume filling factor and overdensity of the ionized regions. In particular, we find that it is difficult to reconcile the observed abundance of voids with models that predict large volume filling factors (f>~0.5) and high overdensities (>~100) for highly ionized proto-cluster regions. direct_prompt: Here is a 9 sentence abstract for the provided article title:Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) provide a means to probe the intergalactic medium (IGM) up to the earliest epochs of the Universe. Using ultraviolet and optical spectroscopy of GRB afterglows with large ground-based telescopes, the absorption signatures of intervening material can be detected. In this study we analyze high-resolution spectra of 10 GRB sightlines to investigate the incidence and properties of carbon IV (C IV) absorbers. We detect a total of 19 C IV systems along these lines of sight covering redshifts from 1.5 to 3.5. The number density of C IV absorbers is found to be consistent with previous quasar absorption line studies over the same redshift range. The derived C IV column density distribution also agrees well with prior measurements from quasar spectra. However, we find tentative evidence for an excess of weak C IV absorbers (log NC IV < 13.5) in GRB spectra compared to quasars. Potential explanations for this result, such as an enhanced ionizing radiation field near GRB hosts, are discussed. Overall, our absorption line study reveals broad consistency between the C IV populations observed toward GRBs and quasars, supporting the use of GRBs as probes of the high-redshift IGM.

title: Orbital degeneracy removed by charge order in triangular antiferromagnet  AgNiO2
direct_prompt: Here is a 5 sentence abstract for the provided article title:Orbital degeneracy removed by charge order in triangular antiferromagnet AgNiO2Transition metal oxides with geometrically frustrated triangular lattices can exhibit unusual electronic and magnetic properties due to competing interactions. AgNiO2 is a rare example of a triangular antiferromagnet, whose Ni2+ ions form a triangular lattice in the ab plane. Previous work has shown that AgNiO2 undergoes simultaneous charge ordering and antiferromagnetic transitions below 230 K. In this study, we use resonant x-ray diffraction to directly observe the charge ordering propagation vector in AgNiO2. Our results demonstrate that the charge ordering lifts the orbital degeneracy of the Ni2+ ions below the transition, thereby removing geometric frustration and allowing antiferromagnetic ordering to occur.

We used a combination of experimental and computational methods to explore the growth window and possible mechanism of millimeter-thick SWCNT forests. Our results show that the growth of thick SWCNT forests is limited by the availability of catalyst sites and the diffusion of carbon atoms. We observed that the growth rate decreases with increasing forest height, indicating a decrease in the number of available catalyst sites. Our density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that the bonding between the SWCNTs and the catalyst surface plays a crucial role in the growth mechanism. We found that the SWCNTs preferentially grow on the catalyst surface through a hydrogen-mediated mechanism, which allows for the formation of thick forests with uniform properties. Our findings provide new insights into the growth mechanism of SWCNT forests and pave the way for the large-scale synthesis of high-quality SWCNT materials.

direct_prompt: Stochastic genetic circuits are a crucial component of many biological systems, and their behavior is inherently uncertain due to the random fluctuations of molecular interactions. However, recent advances in experimental and computational techniques have enabled the deterministic characterization of these stochastic circuits. We discuss the challenges associated with characterizing stochastic circuits and highlight the benefits of using deterministic approaches, such as increased predictive power and improved understanding of circuit behavior. We also provide examples of how deterministic characterization has led to a deeper understanding of biological systems, including the regulatory networks of gene expression and the behavior of swarming bacteria. Furthermore, we discuss the potential applications of deterministic characterization in the design and engineering of biological systems, including the optimization of gene therapies and the development of novel biotechnologies. Overall, this review highlights the growing interest in deterministic approaches to characterizing stochastic genetic circuits and their potential to revolutionize our understanding of biological systems.

In this study, we developed a deterministic approach to characterize stochastic genetic circuits, which allows us to quantify their behavior and identify key design principles. title: Dust Formation and He II 4686 emission in the Dense Shell of the  Peculiar Type Ib Supernova 2006jc
direct_prompt: The peculiar Type Ib supernova 2006jc has been the subject of much study due to its unique properties, including a dense shell and strong He II 4686 emission. In this study, we investigate the dust formation and He II 4686 emission in the dense shell of SN 2006jc using a combination of observational and theoretical methods. We analyze a set of spectra obtained at various epochs and find that the He II 4686 emission is most prominent in the early stages of the supernova's evolution. We also observe a significant increase in the dust production rate around day 200, which we attribute to the formation of a dense shell. Using radiative transfer modeling, we demonstrate that the observed He II 4686 emission can be explained by the presence of a dense shell, and that the dust production rate is consistent with the expected rate for a Type Ib supernova. Our findings provide insight into the physical processes that occur in the dense shells of peculiar Type Ib supernovae, and highlight the importance of considering dust formation and radiation transfer in studies of these events.

title: Outer jet X-ray and radio emission in R Aquarii: 1999.8 to 2004.0
direct_prompt: The radio and X-ray light curves of the symbiotic recurrent nova R Aquarii (R Aqr) during its 1999.8 and 2004.0 outbursts are presented. The light curves at both wavelengths consist of three major components. The first component, lasting for the first ∼100 days, is due to the synchrotron self-absorption (SSA) of the expanding ejecta. It is followed by a power-law decay that might be due to the synchrotron radiation of the expanding ejecta in the adiabatic phase and/or a jet. The last component is the quiescent emission from the companion star or a jet. The mass of the ejecta is estimated to be (6.7 ± 1.1) × 10^−5 Msun. The kinetic energy of the ejecta is estimated to be (3.8 ± 0.7) × 10^42 erg. The initial expansion velocity of the ejecta is estimated to be (2760 ± 440) km s^−1. It is confirmed that two prominent radio lobes along the jet were formed during the 2000.5 event. It is suggested that the jet was launched after the interaction of the expanding ejecta with the red giant wind and that the synchrotron radiation of the jet in the adiabatic phase mainly contributes to the second component of the radio and X-ray light curves.

title: CCD BV survey of 42 open clusters
direct_prompt:
This paper presents the results of a CCD BV survey conducted on 42 open clusters in the Milky Way galaxy. The survey aimed to determine the age, distance, and metallicity of these clusters using photometric data. The observations were carried out using a 4-m telescope equipped with a CCD camera, allowing for precise measurements of the brightness and color of the cluster stars. The data were analyzed using stellar evolution models to derive the fundamental parameters of the clusters, such as age and metallicity. Our results show a wide range of ages and metallicities among the clusters, indicating a diverse formation history of these stellar groups.

Additionally, we found several clusters with unusual properties, such as extended tails or multiple populations. These findings provide valuable insights into the star formation history and dynamics of open clusters in the Milky Way. The cluster distances derived from our survey data were compared with previous studies, showing good agreement and validating the accuracy of our measurements. Furthermore, we identified several clusters that deviate significantly from the standard isochrones, suggesting the presence of unresolved binary or variable stars.

The implications of these findings for our understanding of cluster evolution and star formation processes are discussed. We also provide a comprehensive catalog of the fundamental parameters for each of the 42 clusters surveyed, which can serve as a valuable resource for future studies. Overall, this CCD BV survey has significantly improved our knowledge of the properties and characteristics of open clusters in the Milky Way, shedding light on their formation and evolution.

Previous observations had shown these galaxies to have quiescent nuclei with no signs of ongoing accretion activity. The flares had durations ranging from tens of minutes to a few hours and showed hard power-law spectra characteristic of accreting black holes. We consider possible physical origins for these flares including the tidal disruption of asteroids or minor mergers sending material towards the nuclear supermassive black holes. Such events provide a rare glimpse into low-level activity from galactic nuclei that are otherwise quiescent. Further observations are needed to characterize the frequency and energetics of such flare events from normal galaxies. Understanding transient nuclear activity has implications for establishing the duty cycles of growth phases of supermassive black holes across cosmic history.

direct_prompt: Here is a 6 sentence abstract for the article title "The Distribution of AGN in Clusters of Galaxies":Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are found throughout the universe, however their distribution within galaxy clusters is not well understood. This study analyzes observational data from X-ray and radio surveys to identify AGN located within hundreds of galaxy clusters. The positions and luminosities of detected AGN are compared to properties of their host clusters such as galaxy number, mass, and spatial distribution. Preliminary results suggest that brighter AGN prefer clusters with fewer member galaxies and lower masses. Further analysis is needed to better understand whether cluster environment plays a role in triggering or suppressing AGN activity. This work aims to provide new insights into the connection between galaxy cluster evolution and growth of supermassive black holes.

title: Phase resolved measurements of stimulated emission
direct_prompt: Phase-resolved measurements of stimulated emission provide detailed information about the dynamics of charge carriers in semiconductors. In this work, we present a new technique for performing phase-resolved measurements of stimulated emission that is based on a combination of time-resolved photoluminescence and pump-probe spectroscopy. This technique allows us to measure the phase of the stimulated emission signal with respect to the phase of the pump pulse, which provides information about the lifetime of the charge carriers and the dynamics of the recombination process. We demonstrate the application of our technique to the study of GaAs quantum wells and show that it can be used to extract accurate values for the carrier lifetime and the recombination rate. Our technique is a powerful tool for studying the dynamics of charge carriers in semiconductors and can be used to investigate a wide range of phenomena, such as carrier transport, recombination, and relaxation.

The pulses are generated by actively modulating the current and hence the optical gain in a small section of an edge-emitting quantum cascade laser.

At low temperatures, a large magnetic entropy change (-ΔSM) and a refrigerant capacity (RC) of 171.3 J/kg K and 430.2 J/kg for x = 0.5 have been obtained, respectively, under a magnetic field change of 5 T. By understanding the factors that govern these transitions, we can gain insights into the behavior of complex fluids at the nanoscale. These findings have important implications for the design and control of materials with tailored properties in various applications. Overall, our study contributes to the fundamental understanding of capillary ordering and layering transitions in two-dimensional hard-rod fluids.

Only an upper limit to its optical luminosity has been set (m_R > 22.5). In this paper, we use new Hubble Space Telescope (HST) data to place much tighter constraints on the optical counterpart. From the HST/ACS images in the F435W and F814W bands, we have identified five point sources within the Chandra error circle. Four of them are located in the crowded field and are most likely background sources not associated with the ULX, while the fifth one (hereafter X-1-opt) stands out as a good candidate to be the optical counterpart of NGC300 X-1. It is located 0\farcs25 away from the Chandra position, and has magnitudes of m_F435W = 23.96+/-0.10 and m_F814W = 23.34+/-0.09. From the spectral energy distribution (SED) of the candidate and comparison with evolutionary synthesis models, we find that X-1-opt is most likely a luminous blue variable (LBV) star. We estimate its mass to be in the range between 50 and 100 Msun and its age of similar or slightly less than 10 Myr. The inferred properties, e.g. mass, luminosity, and evolutionary stage, make X-1-opt a very interesting candidate to produce the X-rays via colliding winds, either as a single massive star or in a binary system.

The model incorporates unitarization techniques to account for the strong coupling between various channels. By including contributions from meson-baryon and baryon-baryon interactions, we are able to accurately describe the scattering amplitudes in this energy range. Our model is based on a set of coupled integral equations that solve for the scattering matrix elements for each channel. We compare our results to experimental data and find good agreement in the resonance region. The inclusion of dynamical effects leads to a more realistic description of the $\pi N$ scattering process. We also investigate the impact of different resonance parameters on the scattering observables and discuss the implications for our understanding of nucleon resonances. Overall, our coupled-channel model provides a valuable tool for studying $\pi N$ scattering dynamics in the low to intermediate energy region.

direct_prompt: In this paper, we present recent results on the thermal Casimir force between dielectrics and various related problems. We discuss the effects of temperature on the Casimir force between dielectric materials, including both attractive and repulsive contributions. Our analysis includes the impact of material properties, geometry, and temperature on the thermal Casimir force. Additionally, we explore the role of surface roughness and corrugation on the Casimir force in dielectric systems. We also investigate the influence of non-local effects and finite temperature corrections on the Casimir force. Furthermore, we discuss experimental implications and potential applications of the Casimir force in dielectric systems. Our findings provide valuable insights into the thermal Casimir force between dielectrics and contribute to the understanding of fundamental interactions at the nanoscale. Overall, this research contributes to the current knowledge and future developments in the field of Casimir physics and quantum fluctuation-induced forces. Our results have implications for various technological applications, such as nanotechnology and MEMS devices, where Casimir forces play a significant role. In conclusion, our study sheds light on the complexities of the thermal Casimir force between dielectrics and opens up avenues for further investigation and theoretical advancements in the field.

One approach, followed by Polyakov, is to use a path integral approach. This approach requires the specification of a world sheet action and a measure for the path integral. A particularly interesting alternative action is the sigma model action, which is proportional to the integral of the square root of the determinant of the induced metric on the world sheet.The sigma model action has a number of advantages over the Polyakov action. First, it is well-defined for all values of the string coupling. Second, it is conformally invariant, which means that it is invariant under changes of the metric on the world sheet. Third, it is related to string field theory, which is a perturbative approach to string theory.In this paper, we will study the sigma model action in the tensionless limit. This limit is obtained by taking the string tension to zero. In this limit, the sigma model action reduces to a two-dimensional topological field theory.We will show that the sigma model in the tensionless limit is equivalent to a particular two-dimensional topological field theory known as the Liouville theory. This equivalence will allow us to use the methods of Liouville theory to study the sigma model.

title: 2MASS Reveals a Large Intrinsic Fraction of BALQSOs
direct_prompt: In this study, we report the results of our investigation into the fraction of broad-absorption-line quasars (BALQSOs) that exhibit intrinsic absorption. Using data from the 2-Micron All-Sky Survey (2MASS), we have identified a large sample of BALQSOs and analyzed their spectral energy distributions (SEDs) to determine the fraction of objects with intrinsic absorption. Our results show that a significant fraction of BALQSOs ( approximately 60%) exhibit intrinsic absorption, which is indicative of the presence of dust and gas within the vicinity of the supermassive black hole (SMBH) at the center of the quasar. We find that the intrinsic fraction of BALQSOs is dependent on the luminosity of the quasar, with more luminous objects exhibiting a higher fraction of intrinsic absorption. Furthermore, we discover that the intrinsic fraction of BALQSOs is also dependent on the orientation of the quasar, with objects viewed at smaller angles exhibiting a higher fraction of intrinsic absorption. Our findings suggest that the presence of dust and gas close to the SMBH is a common feature of quasars and may play a crucial role in the evolution of these objects.

We show that the dHvA oscillations in nanowires are strongly affected by the size and shape of the nanowires, as well as by the magnetic field orientation. Our results provide a comprehensive understanding of the dHvA effect in metallic nanowires and pave the way for using dHvA measurements to characterize the electronic properties of nanowires.

title: Cosmogenic neutrinos as a probe of the transition from Galactic to  extragalactic cosmic rays
direct_prompt: Cosmic rays are high-energy particles originating from sources beyond our solar system, with their exact origins and properties remaining a subject of intense interest in astrophysics. In this study, we examine the role of cosmogenic neutrinos as a potential probe of the transition from Galactic to extragalactic cosmic rays. Neutrinos are unique in their ability to travel long distances without significant interaction, allowing them to provide information about cosmic ray sources across vast distances. By studying the energy spectrum and arrival directions of cosmogenic neutrinos, we can gain insights into the mechanisms responsible for cosmic ray acceleration in both Galactic and extragalactic environments. Our analysis suggests that the transition from Galactic to extragalactic cosmic rays may be associated with changes in the neutrino flux at high energies. We also investigate the potential implications of our findings for understanding the distribution of cosmic ray sources in the Universe. Our results highlight the importance of using multiple messengers, including neutrinos, to further our understanding of the cosmic ray landscape. Overall, cosmogenic neutrinos offer a valuable tool for studying the mechanisms driving the production and propagation of cosmic rays on a cosmic scale.

direct_prompt: Dimer models have been introduced to describe free fermions and their interactions. They have been also used in super quantum mechanics. The proposed dimer model provides a new approach to study free fermions and their interactions.

We show that the dimer models can be mapped to free fermions with attractive nearest-neighbor interactions, and the ground-state wave function of the dimer models can be written as a Pfaffian of the fermion operators. We also show that the dimer models are related to supersymmetric quantum mechanics, and the ground-state energy of the dimer models can be obtained from the zero-point energy of the corresponding supersymmetric Hamiltonian. We apply our results to study the dimer models on the square lattice, the honeycomb lattice, and the kagome lattice. We obtain exact results for the ground-state energy, the excitation spectrum, and the correlation functions of the dimer models on these lattices. Our results provide a new perspective on the dimer models and their applications in statistical physics, quantum chemistry, and condensed matter physics.

title: Physically Sound Hamiltonian Formulation of the Dynamical Casimir Effect
direct_prompt: Here is a 10 sentence abstract for the provided article title:The dynamical Casimir effect occurs when vacuum fluctuations in quantum field theory produce real particles from a boundary undergoing nonuniform acceleration. Previous studies have modeled this effect using approximate methods that did not fully consider its inherently relativistic nature. This paper presents a physically sound Hamiltonian formulation of the dynamical Casimir effect for a massless scalar field with a time-dependent boundary condition in 1+1 dimensions. The formulation is based on standard canonical quantization of a relativistic scalar field in terms of creation and annihilation operators. Equations of motion for the field operators are derived and exact solutions for particle creation are obtained in terms of Bogoliubov coefficients. It is shown that the number of created particles can be computed unambiguously from the Hamiltonian and agrees with results from other formalisms under appropriate limits. Notably, this approach allows the backreaction of created particles on the boundary dynamics to be incorporated self-consistently. The new formulation provides a technically rigorous foundation for studying effects like particle creation across accelerating mirrors and their applications in analog gravity systems.

title: Fast recursive filters for simulating nonlinear dynamic systems
direct_prompt: Nonlinear dynamic systems are prevalent in various fields such as control theory, robotics, and signal processing. To accurately simulate these systems, fast recursive filters are often utilized due to their computational efficiency. This paper proposes a novel approach for designing fast recursive filters that can efficiently model the nonlinear dynamics of complex systems. The proposed filters achieve high simulation accuracy while maintaining low time complexity, making them suitable for real-time applications. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed filters in accurately simulating the behavior of nonlinear dynamic systems. Additionally, comparative analysis with existing filter designs shows the superior performance of the proposed filters in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. Overall, the proposed fast recursive filters offer a promising solution for simulating nonlinear dynamic systems in real-time applications.

title: Functional renormalization for quantum phase transitions with  non-relativistic bosons
direct_prompt: Functional renormalization group (FRG) provides a powerful non-perturbative approach to study quantum phase transitions. In this paper, we extend the FRG method to Bose systems with non-relativistic dispersion and study the superfluid-Mott insulator transition in two dimensions. We derive the FRG flow equations for the effective average action and analyze the critical properties of the transition. We show that non-relativistic dispersion leads to significant quantitative and qualitative changes in the critical behavior compared to the relativistic case. In particular, the critical exponents and the shape of the critical line are different. Our results provide a better understanding of the superfluid-Mott insulator transition in systems with non-relativistic bosons, such as ultracold atomic gases and superconductors.

The results for the critical temperature and the critical exponents are discussed and compared to other approaches.

Our results show that increasing the number of nodes in an RBN leads to a decrease in average sensitivity, suggesting a more stable system. Furthermore, we find that higher levels of connectivity can increase the average sensitivity, indicating a more chaotic behavior within the network. These findings provide valuable insights into the relationship between network structure and system stability in RBNs. Overall, our analysis contributes to the understanding of complex systems and highlights the importance of the average sensitivity as a tool for studying dynamics in RBNs.

direct_prompt: The structures and energetics of $^3$He and $^4$He nanodroplets doped with alkaline earth atoms (Ca, Sr, and Ba) are investigated using first-principles calculations. The geometries of the doped droplets with one to six alkaline earth atoms are optimized at the B3LYP/aug-cc-pVTZ level of theory. The binding energies, second-order energy differences, ionization energies, and atomization energies are computed for the most stable isomers of the doped droplets. The calculated results show that the alkaline earth atoms are encapsulated inside the helium droplets for all the sizes considered. The binding energies of alkaline earth atoms increase with increasing the droplet size and the atomic number of the dopant. The second-order energy differences indicate that the doped droplets are fluxional and the most stable isomers may not necessarily be the global minima. The ionization energies of the doped droplets decrease with increasing the droplet size and the atomic number of the dopant. The atomization energies of the doped droplets are positive, indicating that the evaporation of alkaline earth atoms from the droplets is endothermic.

Previous work has developed a geometric prescription for computing RG flow to first order in perturbation theory using a worldsheet metric. In this paper, we extend this framework to all orders in perturbation theory by defining a new metric on the space of worldsheet theories. We show that this "RG flow metric" remains tractable to compute to higher orders and satisfies all the properties required to yield canonical RG flow. As an application, we derive a concise flow equation governing worldsheet theories near their non-perturbative fixed points. Our metric provides new insights into the globally geometric structure of RG flow beyond the usual perturbative regime. This rigorous framework should enable further non-perturbative studies of renormalization group behavior in two-dimensional quantum field theories.

direct_prompt: The Galactic Center (GC) diffuse X-ray emission is one of the most prominent features in the central region of our Galaxy. The X-ray emission is thought to be produced by thermal emission from hot plasma and non-thermal emission from cosmic rays.The relative contribution of these two components is still a matter of debate. In this work, we perform a differential absorption/emission analysis of the GC diffuse X-ray emission using Suzaku observations. We find that the non-thermal emission dominates the GC diffuse X-ray emission in the inner region (r < 50 pc), while the thermal emission becomes more significant in the outer region (r > 50 pc). Our results suggest that the GC diffuse X-ray emission is likely produced by a combination of thermal and non-thermal processes.

By comparing the hard X-ray spectrum measured by _INTEGRAL_ with that obtained by _RXTE_, we confirm the previously reported evidence for a significant decrease of the \(\sim\)6.4 keV iron K emission line intensity in the recent years. The most straightforward explanation of this finding is a partial covering of the hard X-ray source by cold material. The observed column density, however, appears to be too high for the partial covering scenario. The decrease of the iron line intensity might also be caused by a decrease of the hard X-ray flux and/or by a variability of the iron line emission itself. direct_prompt: In this study, we investigate the role of Comptonization in shaping the spectra of accretion-powered X-ray pulsars. We analyze a sample of 10 pulsars, using a combination of observations from the NuSTAR and Swift satellites. We find that the spectra of these pulsars are characterized by a power-law continuum, with a high energy cutoff at around 20 keV, and a strong iron line at 6.4 keV. We demonstrate that the spectra can be well-described by a Comptonization model, with a high electron temperature and optical depth. We also find that the strength of the iron line is correlated with the pulsar's spin-down luminosity, suggesting a link between the accretion rate and the strength of the magnetic field. Our results provide new insights into the physics of accretion-powered X-ray pulsars, and highlight the importance of Comptonization in shaping their spectra.

Through computational experiments, we verify that our algorithms perform significantly better than prior work in practice. Our techniques may help enable more efficient lossless data compression in cases where letter costs are relevant, such as when coding texts in different languages. Overall, this work contributes new algorithmic and analytical tools for optimizing prefix-free coding with unequal letter costs.

title: A balanced memory network
direct_prompt: This paper proposes a novel approach to memory management in artificial intelligence systems, termed the Balanced Memory Network (BMN). The BMN combines the strengths of both episodic and semantic memory systems to create a more efficient and effective memory management system. The BMN is designed to balance the trade-off between the flexibility of episodic memory and the stability of semantic memory, allowing the system to adapt to changing contexts while maintaining a consistent sense of self.The BMN is composed of three main components: an episodic memory module, a semantic memory module, and a memory balancing module. The episodic memory module is responsible for storing and retrieving specific, detailed information about past events, while the semantic memory module stores and retrieves general knowledge and facts. The memory balancing module acts as a mediator between the two, allocating the appropriate amount of resources to each module based on the current context.The BMN is evaluated on several tasks, including memory recall, problem-solving, and decision-making. The results show that the BMN outperforms traditional memory management systems in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability. The BMN also demonstrates improved ability to handle conflicting information and to learn from experience.Further analysis reveals that the BMN's ability to balance between episodic and semantic memory is key to its success. The system is able to adapt to changing contexts by adjusting the allocation of resources between the two memory modules, allowing it to effectively handle tasks that require both short-term and long-term memory.Overall, the Balanced Memory Network presents a significant advancement in the field of memory management in artificial intelligence. Its ability to balance between episodic and semantic memory allows it to effectively handle a wide range of tasks and contexts, making it a valuable tool for a variety of applications.

In this paper, we study the standard forms and entanglement engineering of multimode Gaussian states under local operations. We first derive a complete set of local unitary operations that can be used to transform any multimode Gaussian state into its standard form, where the state is diagonal in the Fock basis. We then show how these local unitary operations can be used to engineer entanglement between different modes of a multimode Gaussian state. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for quantum information processing and communication.

direct_prompt: **Abstract**: We present a general framework for the calculation of maximally supersymmetric planar Yang-Mills amplitudes at five loops. The method is based on a combination of the integrand reduction method and the loop-by-loop approach, where the integrand reduction is performed in the five-dimensional maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory in dimensional regularization and the loop integrals are calculated in the four-dimensional theory. We derive the five-loop integrands for all MHV and NMHV amplitudes and give explicit results for the five-loop MHV amplitudes. We demonstrate the cancellation of all ultraviolet and infrared divergences by explicitly calculating the two-loop and three-loop MHV amplitudes as well as the two-loop NMHV amplitudes in dimensional regularization in four dimensions. We also perform checks of our results against the known five-loop MHV amplitude in the literature.

Tests on known (anti)ferromagnetic samples, including various nickel, cobalt and iron alloys, show the new technique can determine magnetic susceptibility to within 1% accuracy. In summary, this novel and precise technique extends our ability to probe magnetic properties and holds promise for advancing the understanding and development of (anti)ferromagnetic materials.

title: The CoRoT primary target HD 52265: models and seismic tests
direct_prompt: The seismic properties of solar-type stars are key ingredients to test stellar models. Asteroseismic space missions like CoRoT have contributed to significantly improve our knowledge in this field. We present in this article the seismic modeling of HD 52265, which is one of the two primary targets of the CoRoT space mission. We compare the predictions from stellar models computed with the STAREVOL code with the seismic properties derived from the space observations. The seismic constraints on the internal structure of the star are obtained thanks to a dedicated inversion method. These seismic constraints are compared with the predictions of three sets of stellar models, computed by three different teams. The seismic models are in agreement for most of the global stellar parameters. However, significant differences appear between the models concerning the internal structure. In particular, models exhibit significant differences in the central density and in the depth of the convective envelope. The comparison with the seismic inferences allows us to discriminate between these models and shows that none of them is able to fully reproduce the seismic constraints. In particular, we confirm that models suffer from a general difficulty to simultaneously fit the large frequency separation and the frequency of maximum power. The discrepancies between models and observations suggest potential problems either in the modeling of the physics of stellar interiors or in the determination of the seismic properties.
prompt_few_shot: The star HD 52265, observed for 150 days by CoRoT during its first run, is one of the best targets to test asteroseismic modeling. Using the scaling relations, global seismic parameters have been estimated: the large frequency separation, the frequency of maximum power, and the small frequency separations. We computed grids of stellar models (without and with overshooting, for various values of the mixing length parameter) in order to compare their seismic properties to the observations. We show that models without overshooting (or with a very small value of the mixing length parameter) are favored to interpret the observations. Moreover, using a Monte Carlo approach, we find that some seismic constraints can be used to reduce considerably the uncertainties on stellar parameters. For this specific target, our seismic analysis confirms the high helium abundance derived from spectroscopy. We estimate its mass and age to be 1.15+/- 0.05 Msun and 4.4+/- 0.7 Gyr. The additional seismic constraints allow us to reduce significantly the error bars on the radius (by a factor 3) and on the surface helium abundance (by a factor 4).
prompt_SICO: **Abstract**HD 52265 is one of the main targets observed by the CoRoT space mission in long run. The star is a F-type main sequence star located at 120 pc from the Sun. It is known to pulsate in several pressure (p) modes that were identified by means of ground-based observations, and also detected by space photometry with unprecedented quality thanks to the CoRoT satellite. We present in this paper a seismic analysis based on new evolutionary models computed with the GARSTA code that account for mixed overshooting in the convective core, and microscopic diffusion. A comparison with models where these processes are ignored shows that they are required to properly reproduce the observed oscillation frequencies. We present also an asteroseismic analysis performed with the pulsation codes ADIPLS and GYRE to constrain the internal properties of the star, including the evolutionary status, the core overshoot, and the surface helium abundance. We obtain a best model with a mass of 1.353 Msun, a radius of 1.617 Rsun, a luminosity of 3.14 Lsun, an age of 2.53 Gyr, and a core overshoot parameter of 0.11 pressure scale heights. title: Cascading on extragalactic background light
direct_prompt: Here is a 12 sentence abstract for the article titled "Cascading on extragalactic background light":The extragalactic background light (EBL) permeating the universe can interact with high-energy photons from distant gamma-ray sources through photon-photon collision. This interaction leads to cascade processes that reprocess the initial gamma-ray photons to lower energies. In this study, we investigate the impact of these cascades initiated by interactions with the EBL. Using the latest EBL models, we simulate gamma-ray photon propagation over cosmological distances and the resulting cascade development. Our simulations follow the production and propagation of electron-positron pairs, as well as the upscattering and pair-production processes that give rise to subsequent cascade generations. We find significant modifications to the observed gamma-ray spectra of sources beyond redshifts of 0.5, with attenuation increasing with both energy and redshift. The cascade processes predominantly act to soften observed spectra through the down-scattering of gamma-rays. Our results indicate that accounting for these cascades is important for correctly interpreting measurements of distant gamma-ray sources. We discuss the implications of our findings for observations with current and future gamma-ray observatories. Accounting for EBL cascading will be crucial for using very high energy gamma-rays to study cosmology and fundamental physics in the coming years.

title: Two-dimensional Ising model with competing interactions and its  application to clusters and arrays of $\pi$-rings and adiabatic quantum  computing
direct_prompt: Two-dimensional Ising models with competing interactions on square lattices have been studied. The ground-state phase diagram of the model is obtained by using the Wang-Landau Monte Carlo simulation. We found that a variety of the magnetic structures such as a noncollinear antiferromagnetic order, a collinear antiferromagnetic order, a ferrimagnetic order, and a spin-flop state appear in the phase diagram. The nature of magnetic phase transitions was analyzed by the magnetic susceptibility, the specific heat, and the Binder's fourth-order cumulant. It is revealed that quantum effects are enhanced for the case with the noncollinear antiferromagnetic order. It is found that the model is mapped onto the classical XY model with the Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interaction and the symmetric exchange anisotropy, and the properties of low-energy excitations of the model were investigated by using the spin-wave theory. The magnetic properties of clusters and arrays of $\pi$-rings with the competing interactions were investigated by using the exact diagonalization and the Monte Carlo simulation. The energy gaps for low-lying excited states are estimated for various clusters and arrays of $\pi$-rings, and it is found that arrays of $\pi$-rings with the competing interactions can be a candidate for adiabatic quantum computing.

For a two-dimensional square lattice of $\pi$-rings, magnetic phase diagrams and magnetization curves are presented. The influence of the quantum effects and the inter-ring distance on the magnetic properties of arrays of $\pi$-rings is investigated.

title: Spin transport in magnetic multilayers
direct_prompt: Here is a 12 sentence abstract for the article titled "Spin transport in magnetic multilayers":Spin transport properties in magnetic multilayered structures continue to be an important area of study due to their potential applications in spin electronic devices. In this work, we investigate current-induced spin transport effects in trilayer structures composed of ferromagnetic and nonmagnetic metal thin films. The trilayer devices are fabricated using sputter deposition with ferromagnetic nickel and cobalt films separated by a nonmagnetic copper spacer layer. Spin injection from the ferromagnetic layers into the copper layer is observed and quantified using giant magnetoresistance measurements at varying current densities. Results indicate that spin accumulation at the ferromagnet/nonmagnet interfaces and efficient spin transport over nanoscale distances can be achieved in these structures. Additional experiments probe the role of spin-orbit coupling and interfacial effects on spin transport over longer length scales. Theoretical modeling of the results is performed to elucidate the underlying physical mechanisms. Our findings provide new insights into intrinsic spin relaxation and spin-memory loss limiting factors in magnetic heterostructures. Implications for developing highly efficient spin valves, magnetic random access memories, and spin logic devices are also discussed. In conclusion, this study enhances understanding of current-induced spin dynamics and spin-dependent transport in magnetic multilayers with potential for future spin-based technologies.

title: Complexity Considerations, cSAT Lower Bound
direct_prompt: This paper explores complexity considerations in the context of constrained Boolean satisfiability (cSAT) problems. We investigate the lower bound of cSAT problems, aiming to understand the inherent difficulty and complexity of these problems. Through theoretical analysis and empirical experimentation, we analyze the factors contributing to the lower bound of cSAT problems. Our results suggest that the lower bound for cSAT problems is highly dependent on the specific problem instance and its structure. We also examine the impact of different problem characteristics on the lower bound, such as clause-to-variable ratio and clause density. Additionally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the design and optimization of algorithms for solving cSAT problems. Our findings shed light on the underlying complexity of cSAT problems and provide insights for future research in this area. Overall, this study contributes to a better understanding of the complexity considerations in cSAT problems and their practical implications for algorithm design and optimization.
